turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on through and I'll get your weight and blood pressure before the doctor sees you. Shoes off, if you don't mind.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh God, the scales. Is it going to be desperate? I've been putting this off for weeks.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): You're 84 kilograms. Blood pressure is 146 over 84, and the pulse is 72. Nothing there for me to fuss over.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): 84? Is that an awful number? And is 146 high? Should I be panicking?
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): I wouldn't panic. The doctor will talk you through the numbers. Have a seat, she won't be a minute.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, come on in and sit wherever's easiest. I'm Dr. Brennan. What's been troubling you?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the knee, doctor. The right one. It's become a pure nuisance, and I'm worried sick about it.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tell me in your own words, then. When do you notice it most?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Going down the stairs is the worst. And at night it aches and I can't get settled. I couldn't date it — last winter, or was it the winter before.
[SEG0010] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm Niamh, her daughter. The stairs at home are steep and she's coming down sideways. She really can't remember when it started.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): You're not thinking it's a tumour, are you? I always go to the worst thing, I'm sorry.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): I can hear the worry, and nothing you've said sounds like that. Is it only the right knee?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Only the right. The left is grand. On the stairs I have to cling to the rail or I feel I'll go.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): And through the night, what sort of pain is it?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): A deep ache. It wakes me two or three times, and I'm wrecked the next day. Is that a bad sign?
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Waking with it matters, yes. Can you put any date at all on when the night pain started?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I can't, doctor. Last winter — well, actually it might have been the one before. It's all mixed up. Does the date matter terribly?
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): It helps, but we can work with it being a good while. What have you tried yourself?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Diclofenac gel, from the chemist. I rub it onto the right knee.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): How often are you putting the gel on?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Twice a day, morning and before bed, just a small amount like the box says. Is the gel dangerous? I read a thing online and it frightened the life out of me.
[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And she has the tablets from the same chemist. Not every day, mind.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, diclofenac, the 50 milligram tablets. I take one on two or three evenings in the week, when the pain is desperate.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any stomach trouble from those tablets?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No, my stomach's grand. Not a bother there at all.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any other medicines? A blood pressure tablet, anything regular?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing else. Will I have to give the gel up? It's the only thing that takes the edge off.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll sort the medicines shortly. Does the knee swell, or give way under you?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No, it doesn't swell, and it doesn't give way. It's stiff in the morning for maybe twenty minutes, then that eases. And I haven't fallen, thank God.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does it ever lock on you, get stuck?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No, it doesn't lock. But will I be needing an operation? That's what I'm really afraid of.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let's not jump to an operation. I'll examine the knee first. Up on the couch when you feel ready.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): The right knee isn't hot and it isn't red. There's crepitus as I bend it, and you're tender along the joint line. The left knee feels normal.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Crepitus, is that the grinding? Does that mean the bone is destroyed? Be straight with me.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): It's rough surfaces moving, very common with wear and tear. You're 84 kilograms today, and that extra load doesn't do a sore knee any favours.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 84 a disaster, then? How much do I have to lose? I don't want to be starving myself.
[SEG0037] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's been doing far less since the knee, and the biscuits have crept in. I say it with love.

[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Nobody is asking you to starve. A small bit of weight off, and keeping gently on the move, takes pressure off the joint. Any heartburn or indigestion? You did say the stomach was fine.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, I do get heartburn. I didn't think of it as a stomach problem. After the tablet, that night, there's a burning up in my chest.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): How often would that come?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Whenever I take the tablet, so two or three times a week. It's not agony. Is it dangerous, though? Should I have said it at the start?
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): You were right to say it now. Stop the diclofenac tablets. Keep using the gel twice a day. For the pain, start paracetamol, one gram by mouth, up to four times a day.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Is paracetamol even strong enough? The gel won't burn the stomach as well, will it? And what if the night pain stays desperate?

[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Paracetamol is the safer one for you with that heartburn, and the gel very rarely upsets the stomach. If the nights stay bad there are other options, but we don't have to choose them today.
[SEG0045] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Her neighbour had an injection in the knee and swore by it. I was wondering about physio as well.

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Both are reasonable. We might send you for physiotherapy, or we might do a steroid injection into the knee, but only if this plan doesn't settle things. We won't decide that today.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Which one is better? Does the injection hurt? Would I manage to walk after, for the bus to mass?

[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): The injection stings for a minute, and most people walk straight out. Physio is exercises, no needle. I can't honestly pick between them for you today, and neither is an operation.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): And you're sure it isn't cancer? I'm sorry for coming back to it.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): From the story and from the examination, this is most likely osteoarthritis, wear and tear in the right knee. I am not worried about a tumour.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Osteoarthritis. Is that with me for life? Will it spread over to the good knee?
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): It can grumble on for years, and the other knee can be affected in time, but the left one is fine today. I'll see you back in six weeks.
[SEG0053] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Will I book the six weeks out at the desk?
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, six weeks with me. Until then it's the gel twice a day, the paracetamol as I said, no more diclofenac tablets, and ease off the biscuits if you can.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): If the heartburn doesn't settle once I stop the tablets, do I ring you, or do I just wait the six weeks?
[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the heartburn is still there after a week or two off the tablets, come back sooner, don't sit on it. Otherwise I'll see you at the six weeks.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Thanks a million, doctor. I came in frightened and I feel a bit calmer, so I do.
